Mechanical string

Words: 37
Continuum mechanics OurBigBook.com
A slender flexible body modeled by a moving curve that transmits tension while its bending stiffness is neglected. For a uniform stretched string with constant tension T and linear mass density μ, small transverse oscillations obey μytt​=Tyxx​; see the wave equation on a string.

Balance of linear momentum (ρDv/Dt=∇⋅σ+ρb)

Words: 30
Continuum mechanics OurBigBook.com
For a body occupying V, the rate of change of ∫V​ρvdV equals the body forces and surface tractions. With the Cauchy stress tensor, the local form is ρDv/Dt=∇⋅σ+ρb.

A yield criterion specifies the admissible elastic stress region, possibly depending on internal hardening variables q. Plastic loading occurs on its boundary. The Tresca yield criterion uses maximum principal-stress difference, while the Von Mises yield criterion uses a quadratic deviatoric-stress invariant. Thus a numerical stress difference must be compared to a yield stress using the convention of the selected criterion.

The stress-strain split, loading conditions and hardening evolution are needed along with this equation to close an elastoplastic model.

Boundary layer

Words: 3k Articles: 33
Continuum mechanics OurBigBook.com
A boundary layer is a thin region next to a surface in which viscosity remains significant even when inertia dominates the outer fluid flow. Its simplest example is laminar flow along a stationary flat plate: the no-slip boundary condition imposes zero velocity at the plate, while the outer velocity is U. The resulting thin velocity profile contains a large normal velocity gradient, so small dynamic viscosity can still produce appreciable wall shear stress. The Blasius boundary layer makes this competition quantitative and explains how a plate aligned with the incoming fluid flow acquires drag.
The same balance appears in a singular perturbation of a differential equation: large derivatives in a thin region can keep a term with a small coefficient significant. For ϵy′′+y′=0 on [0,1] with y(0)=0 and y(1)=1, the inner variable X=x/ϵ resolves a left boundary layer of width O(ϵ).

Blasius boundary layer

Words: 934 Articles: 1
Boundary layer OurBigBook.com
A Blasius boundary layer is the steady flow, two-dimensional laminar flow along a smooth stationary flat plate with uniform outer velocity U>0. Let x>0 measure distance from its leading edge and y≥0 distance normal to its upper face. For a Newtonian fluid with constant mass density ρ and dynamic viscosity μ, write kinematic viscosity ν=μ/ρ. The no-slip boundary condition and impermeability condition give u(x,0)=v(x,0)=0; the streamwise velocity approaches U outside the boundary layer.
For example, choose U=10ms−1 and ν=1.5×10−5m2s−1. At x=0.30m, the local Reynolds number is Rex​=Ux/ν=2.0×105 and the boundary layer thickness is about 3.29mm. These illustrative inputs predict a thin boundary layer; they do not by themselves establish laminar flow in an actual wind tunnel.
The boundary-layer scaling follows by comparing advection, of size U2/x, with normal viscous transport, of size νU/δ2:
δ∼Uνx​​,xδ​∼Rex−1/2​,Rex​=νUx​.
(14)
Equivalently, the available travel time x/U equals the viscous diffusion time δ2/ν in order of magnitude. Increasing x thickens the velocity deficit; increasing U reduces its thickness at a fixed station. This boundary-layer scaling requires Rex​≫1. It cannot resolve the immediate leading-edge region where x is comparable to ν/U.[ref]
The boundary-layer equation assumes a thin, attached laminar flow with streamwise changes over distances much larger than δ, negligible spanwise changes, incompressible flow, and constant material properties. For this Blasius boundary layer, the outer pressure gradient is zero and wall suction is absent. Mass conservation gives v/U=O(δ/x), but vuy​ is still of order U2/x, just like uux​. Thus the Prandtl boundary-layer equation retains both advection terms:
ux​+vy​=0,uux​+vuy​=νuyy​,py​≃0.
(15)
The discarded streamwise viscous term νuxx​ is smaller than νuyy​ by O((δ/x)2). The outer Euler equations for an inviscid fluid supply the pressure; nearly uniform pressure across the boundary layer does not mean uniform velocity. Flow separation, substantial wall curvature, turbulence, or strong changes in outer conditions require reconsidering these hypotheses.
Introduce the stream function and a dimensionless normal coordinate:
η=yνxU​​,ψ=νUx​f(η),u=ψy​=Uf′(η),v=−ψx​=21​xνU​​[ηf′(η)−f(η)].
(16)
Substitution gives the Blasius equation f′′′+ff′′/2=0, with f(0)=f′(0)=0 and f′(∞)=1. Its numerical boundary value problem gives f′′(0)≃0.332057. All streamwise velocity profiles therefore collapse onto the same f′(η) after rescaling y by νx/U​. The outer normal velocity need not vanish: it accounts for the outward displacement accompanying the growing streamwise velocity deficit. The MIT Similarity Solution uses the alternative coordinate ηMIT​=η/2​ and obtains fMIT′′​(0)≃0.46960; its factor of 2​ must be converted before comparing wall shear stress.
The historical Motion of fluids with very little viscosity by L. Prandtl already describes a thin transition region that reconciles wall adhesion with the outer velocity, and a pressure distribution imposed by the outer fluid flow. Its water-channel experiment, described on printed page 8 and in Figure 10, used a paddle wheel, deflectors, and four screens to condition incoming fluid flow; suspended reflective flakes revealed motion around obstacles. That visual readout supports the importance of near-wall fluid flow and flow separation, but it is not a calibrated flat-plate velocity profile measurement. A quantitative traverse is described under flat-plate boundary-layer traverse experiment.

Flat-plate boundary-layer traverse experiment

Words: 452
Blasius boundary layer OurBigBook.com
The Louisiana Tech LAB 8 - Velocity Profile above a Flat Plate describes a 14-inch plate in a wind tunnel. A Pitot-static tube of 0.10-inch outside diameter traverses normally about 12 inches downstream; its screw scale has 0.001-inch increments. A water-column manometer reads the difference between stagnation pressure and static pressure. The procedure establishes a wall position, zeros the tunnel indicator, sets fan speed, and records at least ten positions inside the boundary layer, together with room temperature and barometric pressure. The instrument list includes a flow-stream thermometer implemented with a temperature-sensitive resistor. The manual requests comparison of outer velocity with the tunnel indicator and of the recovered velocity profile with laminar or turbulent predictions; it provides no observed dataset. These are apparatus specifications and instructions, not a reported confirmation of laminar flow.
Under incompressible flow conditions, an ideal aligned Pitot tube gives q(y)=p0​(y)−p(y)=ρu(y)2/2. Convert the manometer head h to q=(ρwater​−ρ)gh, then infer u=2q/ρ​. Here g is gravitational acceleration; mass density ρ can be estimated from temperature and absolute pressure using the ideal gas law. A normalized velocity profile rises from the unresolved near-wall region to a plateau, whose value defines U; downstream profiles should broaden and collapse when plotted against η if the Blasius boundary layer assumptions hold. Integrating a recovered velocity profile gives displacement thickness and momentum thickness.
Additional controls for interpreting this experiment follow from the measurement model: check differential-pressure calibration with equal port pressures and known liquid heads; leak-check tubing; align the Pitot tube with the incoming velocity; convert wall contact to the inlet-centre coordinate rather than treating outside contact as y=0; repeat traverses and outer velocity readings to detect drift. Keep the plate smooth and aligned, and check outer static pressure at multiple downstream stations before assuming zero pressure gradient. Repeating at another station or outer velocity tests the predicted boundary-layer scaling more directly than fitting one curve. These controls are proposed checks, not actions documented as completed in the manual.
Finite probe size, wall interference, flow fluctuations, and weak near-wall dynamic pressure limit inference. Even the manual's probe-based Reynolds number criterion, Red​=ud/ν>1000 for its ideal Bernoulli equation conversion, must be checked with local u, not just U. In the illustrative model at x=0.3048m, δ99​≃3.32mm; the quoted outside diameter is 2.54mm, a substantial fraction of that thickness. A real inlet's sensing footprint and correction cannot be deduced from outside diameter alone. For an ideal footprint that averages dynamic pressure, the inferred velocity is ⟨u2⟩​ rather than ⟨u⟩. Differentiating such sparse readings to obtain wall shear stress magnifies measurement error; the momentum thickness route is less sensitive to this differentiation but still needs the unresolved near-wall contribution. The no-slip boundary condition is a model constraint here, not a direct reading from a probe centred on the wall.

Boundary layer thickness (δ99​)

Words: 260 Articles: 2
Boundary layer OurBigBook.com
The conventional boundary layer thickness δ99​ is the normal distance at which the streamwise velocity first reaches 0.99U in a monotone velocity profile. A Blasius boundary layer approaches U smoothly, so its apparent edge depends on the chosen percentage; there is no discontinuity. Solving f′(η99​)=0.99 in the Blasius equation gives η99​≃4.910, hence
δ99​≃4.910Uνx​​.
(17)
The factor 4.910 belongs to this definition, whereas the boundary-layer scaling specifies only order of magnitude. Near this edge the velocity changes slowly, making a threshold position sensitive to measurement error; displacement thickness and momentum thickness summarize the whole velocity profile.[ref]

Displacement thickness (δ∗)

Words: 61
Boundary layer thickness OurBigBook.com
For constant-mass density incompressible flow, the displacement thickness measures the lost volume flux per unit span divided by the outer velocity:
δ∗=∫0∞​(1−Uu​)dy,Uδ∗=∫0∞​(U−u)dy.
(18)
An outer inviscid flow encountering the same volume flux deficit behaves, at leading order, as though the wall were displaced outward by δ∗. In a Blasius boundary layer, numerical integration gives δ∗≃1.720788νx/U​. This equivalent displacement is smaller than the boundary layer thickness and is not the position of a physical surface.[ref]

Momentum thickness (θ)

Words: 122
Boundary layer thickness OurBigBook.com
The momentum thickness weights the streamwise velocity deficit by the local velocity carrying it:
θ=∫0∞​Uu​(1−Uu​)dy,ρU2θ=ρ∫0∞​u(U−u)dy.
(19)
Thus ρU2θ measures a momentum flux deficit per unit span relative to transporting the same local mass flow rate at U. It is not ρ∫(U2−u2)dy, which compares a different reference flux. A Blasius boundary layer has θ≃0.664115νx/U​; the ratio of displacement thickness to momentum thickness is about 2.591.[ref]
For the steady flow over an impermeable flat plate at constant U, integrating the boundary-layer equation and using mass conservation gives
dxdθ​=ρU2τw​​.
(20)
This connects growth of the momentum thickness to local wall shear stress. Consequently the drag per unit span on one face up to x=L is D′=ρU2θ(L) in the ideal Blasius boundary layer with θ(0)=0. Measured velocity profiles can therefore estimate integrated drag without differentiating noisy near-wall readings. The identity assumes no wall suction and zero outer pressure gradient.[ref]

Wall shear stress (τw​)

Words: 131 Articles: 1
Boundary layer OurBigBook.com
For a stationary flat plate in a Newtonian fluid, the streamwise shear stress exerted by the fluid on its upper face is
τw​=μ∂y∂u​​y=0​.
(21)
The sign here is positive when the fluid pulls the plate downstream; the plate exerts the opposite tangential traction on the fluid. In a Blasius boundary layer, τw​≃0.332057ρU2/Rex​​. A growing boundary layer thickness therefore accompanies decreasing local wall shear stress, because its near-wall velocity gradient becomes gentler. The formal divergence as x→0 is integrable, but that leading-edge limit lies outside the thin-layer hypothesis.[ref]

Wall shear stress OurBigBook.com
The local skin friction coefficient normalizes wall shear stress by the outer dynamic pressure:
cf​(x)=21​ρU2τw​(x)​≃Rex​​0.664115​.
(22)
For the ideal Blasius boundary layer on one face of length L, averaging the local skin friction coefficient gives cf​≃1.328230/ReL​​. The factor of two follows from integrating x−1/2, not from counting both plate faces. Drag on two equally exposed faces doubles when the reference area remains that of one face.

A steady two-dimensional laminar jet driven by force F per span has conserved momentum flux ρ∫u2dy=F. The boundary-layer pressure gradient is zero. Balancing inertia and viscosity with this flux gives width proportional to x2/3 and centre velocity proportional to x−1/3. The streamfunction (Fνx/ρ)1/3f(η), η=y[F/(ρν2x2)]1/3, obeys 3f′′′+(f′)2+ff′′=0. The displayed profile has ∫(f′)2dη=2A3/9, so momentum equality fixes A. Merely requiring independence of x does not fix the amplitude. Entrainment makes volume flux 2A(Fνx/ρ)1/3 grow downstream.

A steady attached laminar boundary layer with slip speed ut​ and downstream distance s has thickness δ∼νs/ut​​. The wall shear is τw​∼μut​/δ, giving the displayed scaling, where μ=ρν is dynamic viscosity. Multiplying by a nearly constant wetted perimeter gives local drag per unit length proportional to ut3/2​s−1/2, and integration gives drag proportional to ut3/2​L​. A force density weighted by s1/2 instead produces L3/2; it can be a separately prescribed phenomenological model but is not this local laminar shear law. Strong curvature, unsteadiness, separation or turbulent transition can invalidate the estimate.

Balancing convection with normal viscous diffusion gives the displayed thickness. With streamfunction Ψ=−Aν​x1/2F(y/δ), xu=Ψy​ and xv=−Ψx​, the similarity equation is F′′′−FF′′/2+2(1−F′2)=0, with F(0)=F′(0)=0 and F′(∞)=1. The displacement-flux correction scales as Aν​R1/2, and the corresponding outer velocity correction as Aν​R−3/2.

For a fluid occupying z<0, match an outer stagnation point flow u=x,w=−z to a flat impermeable interface with dimensionless shear stress βx. With boundary layer thickness δ=Re−1/2, inner variable ζ=z/δ and γ=δβ, the leading boundary-layer equation admits u=xf′(ζ) and w=−δf(ζ). Incompressibility is automatic, and tangential momentum conservation gives the displayed ordinary differential equation, with f(0)=0, f′′(0)=γ and f′→1 at ζ→−∞. The sign of this far-field endpoint is fixed by the fluid domain. This is a prescribed-traction interface; it does not impose a no-slip boundary condition.

Turbulent boundary layer

Words: 426 Articles: 8
Boundary layer OurBigBook.com
A boundary layer in which turbulent velocity fluctuations transport momentum and scalars. A near-wall constant-stress region supports the law of the wall; buoyancy modifies it through Monin-Obukhov similarity theory. A viscous or roughness sublayer and an outer-layer scale bound the range of either approximation.

Turbulent boundary layer OurBigBook.com
The near-wall region where molecular momentum diffusion dominates turbulent transport. Using the shear velocity u∗​=τd​/ρ​ gives the viscous wall length ν/u∗​. The precise extent depends on the chosen crossover criterion and wall condition. In this region constant stress and no slip give U≃u∗2​z/ν; the logarithmic law of the wall applies outside it.

Monin-Obukhov similarity theory (Uz​=κzu∗​​ϕm​(z/ℓO​))

Words: 214 Articles: 3
Turbulent boundary layer OurBigBook.com
A local similarity description for approximately stationary homogeneous surface-layer turbulence with nearly constant momentum and buoyancy fluxes. Besides height and friction velocity, the Obukhov length enters as a stability parameter. The hypothesis fixes the dimensional shear prefactor and function argument, while empirical or dynamical closures determine the functions themselves.
Near-neutral log-linear surface-layer profiles (KM,B​=u∗​zfM,B​(z/ℓ))
Words: 68
Monin-Obukhov similarity theory OurBigBook.com
If the similarity functions of a turbulent boundary layer are differentiable at zero and have finite positive neutral values, expanding f=a+dz/ℓ+O((z/ℓ)2) gives a shear proportional to 1/z−d/(aℓ). Integration yields a logarithmic term plus a linear correction. Dimensional reasoning alone does not fix the coefficients or guarantee this regular neutral limit. The gradient Richardson number is of order z/ℓ, so ∣z/ℓ∣≪1 is a shear-dominated, nearly neutral regime on either side of stability.

In local continuously turbulent scaling at z/ℓO​≫1, dependence on the distance to the wall disappears at leading order. The velocity profile is linear and the buoyancy frequency is constant. Local energy balance gives ϵ=(cm​−1)∣B0​∣ and Rif​=1/cm​, with positive dissipation requiring cm​>1. The coefficients depend on a closure, and this regime should not be imposed on fully collapsed turbulence.

Words: 39
Monin-Obukhov similarity theory OurBigBook.com
The signed wall-turbulence length formed from stress velocity and the vertical turbulent buoyancy flux. With upward buoyancy transport positive, stable cooling has B0​<0 and ℓO​>0; heating from below gives ℓO​<0. The magnitude marks the transition between shear-dominated and buoyancy-dominated scaling.

The dimensionless coefficient in the logarithmic wall law and its mixing-length form ℓ=κz. Its numerical value is determined from the turbulence closure and measurements, rather than from dimensional analysis alone.

The extrapolation height at which a logarithmic wall profile vanishes. For a fully rough wall it is set mainly by the geometry; for a smooth wall it scales with ν/u∗​. It is not the thickness of the molecular viscous sublayer or the literal location of a no-slip surface.

Boundary layer OurBigBook.com
A thermal boundary layer is a thin region in which temperature changes rapidly and thermal conduction remains important. Its thickness can be estimated by balancing thermal diffusion against advection or by requiring a local Rayleigh number to be near its critical value.

In a renewal model, a diffusive thermal boundary layer grows until a convective instability overturns it, after which growth restarts. A layer reaching thickness δ∼κτ​ has mean heat flux of order kΔT/δ. A diffusive t−1/2 flux averaged over one cycle differs only by an order-one coefficient. Distinct thermal and material layers need not share a renewal time.

Acoustic energy flux OurBigBook.com
